questions.question: A service receives 200 requests per second and its average end-to-end time is 0.25 seconds. About how many requests are in flight on average?
questions.explanation: Little's Law gives concurrency = throughput x time: 200 x 0.25 = 50 requests in flight on average.

questions.question: Why can P99 latency rise sharply when a bounded stage reaches 95-100% utilization?
options: The stage becomes faster at high load
New requests wait behind work already in the queue
Percentiles stop measuring latency
The network hop is removed
questions.explanation: Near saturation, there is little spare capacity to absorb variance or bursts, so waiting time grows and affects the tail first.

questions.question: A service accepts 160 RPS but its limiting database can sustainably complete only 140 RPS. What happens if this continues?
options: The queue eventually drains
Latency becomes zero because the database is busy
The queue grows until work is rejected, times out, or demand falls
Throughput immediately becomes 160 RPS
questions.explanation: Arrivals exceed completions by 20 RPS, so queued work accumulates instead of reaching a stable level.

questions.question: Which change is most appropriate for an optional analytics event on a checkout request path?
options: Wait indefinitely for analytics to finish
Move the event to a durable asynchronous queue with an owner and retry policy
Retry the analytics service until checkout times out
Add the analytics work to every database transaction
questions.explanation: The checkout path can meet its user deadline while the durable queue preserves and separately operates the optional work.

questions.question: What is the main latency trade-off of increasing a batch size?
options: Each item may wait for the batch to fill and run
The batch removes all fixed overhead
The system no longer needs capacity
The queue cannot grow
questions.explanation: Larger batches can increase item throughput by amortizing fixed work, but the earliest item waits longer before the batch executes.

questions.question: Why is extending a dependency timeout usually not the first response to a latency incident?
options: It automatically adds database capacity
It can hold workers and connections longer while the dependency is still saturated
It makes P99 impossible to measure
It eliminates the need for deadlines
questions.explanation: Longer waits can consume shared resources and amplify queueing. First determine whether the dependency can actually complete more work per second.
